reply:
**Question frozen.** The paper answers several; the title and opening make this one central: *What can a finite mechanical procedure compute?* Range: binary decimals/sequences computed by an automatic machine from a blank tape, using finite states and finite symbols. Asked: define that class, show what it covers, and show whether a general process can decide if an arbitrary such machine is circle-free — with the Entscheidungsproblem as application.

**Jobs.**
J1 Define “computable” without already assuming the answer.
J2 Show natural numbers (π, e, algebraic, Bessel zeros) are included.
J3 Show computable sequences can be listed.
J4 Build one machine that can run any of them.
J5 Show no general process decides whether a machine is circle-free/satisfactory.
J6 Apply that to the Entscheidungsproblem.
J7 Link to Church’s “effective calculability”.

**Parts, with marks.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Finite set of m-configurations | Held | Remove it; J3 and J5 fail. Infinite states have no finite description to list or diagonalise. |
| Finite alphabet | Held if | J1/J3 need a finite code. Turing says compound symbols can replace many symbols, so the exact alphabet is looser. |
| One-dimensional tape | Loose | Replace with two-dimensional paper plus coding; Turing says the two-dimensional use is avoidable. |
| Automatic (deterministic) machine | Held | J5 needs a fixed sequence from a fixed description. Choice machines can be enumerated by choices, so this is not a hidden extra. |
| Moves: L, R, E, P | Held | Remove one; the simple-operation account of J1 breaks. |
| Circle-free vs circular | Held | Remove it; finite-output machines would be mixed with infinite ones, and J5’s diagonal construction breaks. |
| Standard description / description number | Held | J3 and J5 depend on a finite code for every machine. |
| Universal machine U | Held | J4 and the J5 proof need one machine to simulate a supplied description. |
| Diagonal sequence β′ | Held | Remove it; the contradiction in J5 goes. |
| Reductio using K, the D.N of the testing machine | Held | This is the pivot that forces both verdicts “s” and “u” to fail. |
| §9 intuition arguments | Held if | They hold J1 only if the job “all naturally computable numbers” is accepted. That job is argued, not proved. |
| §10 examples | Held if | They support J2, which is broadness, not the impossibility proof. |
| §11 Entscheidungsproblem reduction | Held if | It holds only if “general process” is accepted as “machine process”. |
| Skeleton-table m-functions | Idle | They are abbreviations; expand the tables and no job is lost. |
| F-squares / E-squares convention | Loose | A coding choice; another tape convention could do the same work. |
| Church equivalence | Borrowed | Rests on Church’s effective calculability, tested elsewhere. |
| Hilbert functional calculus / Peano axioms | Borrowed | Rests on those formal systems. |

**Whole checks.**
*Flip.* Had a deciding machine D existed, the proof would not smoothly explain that too; it derives a contradiction. The broad thesis “all natural computations are machine computations” would be falsified by a counterexample, not absorbed.
*Direction.* The formal part runs forward from machine moves to computed sequences; the impossibility proof assumes a decider and pokes that assumption. It is not merely reading a result backwards.
*Answer hidden?* The formal theorem “no machine decides circle-free” is not circular. The application to *all* effective processes leans on the thesis that any effective process is a machine. That is the main held-if.
*Change list.* Covers: drop finite states/symbols, allow two dimensions, allow B observed squares, allow choice machines, change coding, ask whether a machine prints 0 forever. Leaves out: infinite states, oracles, hypercomputation. The limit is stated: “finite means”.
*Pairs that pull.* Generosity versus enumerability. Allowing B squares or two dimensions is reduced back to the one-tape machine; allowing infinite states would break J3/J5. The line is finite states and symbols. A natural computation not simulable, or a formal gap in the reduction, would show the line is wrong.
*Patches.* Skeleton tables are harmless abbreviation. F/E squares are an explicit coding patch. The §9 intuition arguments are a new supporting thesis, not a proof; the paper says so.
*Rivals.* Church’s lambda calculus and recursive functions are the same at this level: equivalent. A hypercomputer differs only if the change list permits infinite states or oracles; that is a new question.

**Where parts came from.**
The machine model, universal machine, enumeration and diagonal proof are *built*: worked out with the target in view and exposed to counter-case. The §9 thesis is *asserted* and argued, not proved. Church equivalence is *borrowed*. The Entscheidungsproblem is a borrowed problem with a built reduction.

**What would make it harder to vary.**
1. Prove or sharply limit the thesis that every effective process is a machine, or show equivalence with several independent models.
2. Test the finite-state/finite-symbol line directly: either exhibit a natural finite-means computation outside the class, or complete the reduction from general observed-square machines in full detail.

**What this does not show.**
Hard to vary is not true. The formal theorem is tight. The application to “all possible processes” rests on an intuitive thesis. The paper does not prove the Church–Turing thesis; it defines one precise class and shows its limits.

**One next step.**
Take the one doubtful job — J1’s “all naturally computable numbers” — and try to build a counterexample under the paper’s own changes. If none appears, mark it *held if* the thesis is accepted, not *held*.
